plan.title: Why too large a learning rate makes gradient descent blow up
plan.description: A ball sits on a bowl-shaped loss surface that is steep in one direction and gentle in the other. Each step, the ball moves downhill by the learning rate times the slope, leaving a trail and showing an arrow for the step it is about to take. With a small learning rate the trail creeps into the bottom of the bowl. Past a critical value it overshoots to the far side, lands higher than it started, and each jump gets bigger until it leaves the surface.
plan.reason: Divergence makes sense when you move the learning rate across the tipping point yourself and watch the same start either settle or bounce outward. The readouts show the exact number that decides which happens.
interactions: Play to let the ball take steps one after another, or pause and take one step at a time
Lower the learning rate below the critical value and watch the trail settle into the bottom instead of bouncing outward
Raise the steepness and watch the critical learning rate fall, so a rate that worked before now diverges
Read the loss, the step count, the critical rate and the stretch factor for the steep direction on each step
Orbit the camera to see the zig-zag from above or from the side
assumptions: Illustration: an idealised bowl-shaped loss, not a real trained model.
Loss is half of (gentle direction squared plus steepness times steep direction squared); the gentle direction has steepness 1.
Each step moves the ball by minus the learning rate times the slope, with no momentum and no noise.

Along the steep direction, each step multiplies the distance from the bottom by (1 minus learning rate times steepness). If that factor's size is above 1, the distance grows every step. That happens when the learning rate is above 2 divided by the steepness. This is exact for this bowl.
Every run starts at the same point, partway up both slopes. The run stops when the ball leaves the drawn surface (marked as diverged), when the loss falls below 0.001 (converged), or after 60 steps.
Surface heights are scaled down so steep settings still fit on screen; the readouts show the true loss.
limitations: Real loss surfaces are not perfect bowls, so their critical learning rate is only roughly 2 divided by the steepest curvature (how sharply the slope bends) near the current point, and it changes as training moves.

With steepness 1, the critical rate is 2, which is above this slider's top value, so that setting never diverges here. Higher steepness brings the tipping point into range (0.5 at the default steepness of 4).
Right at the critical value the ball bounces back and forth forever without growing or shrinking. Rounding of numbers may make it drift slightly.
plan.learningGoal: A step overshoots the minimum when the learning rate times the curvature is more than 2. Each overshoot then lands farther from the bottom than the last, so the loss grows instead of shrinking.

draft.title: Why too large a learning rate makes gradient descent blow up
draft.description: A blue bowl-shaped loss surface, steep along left-right (x) and gentle along front-back (z). A red ball does gradient descent from the same start each run, leaving an orange trail; an orange arrow shows its next step. A small dark dot marks the lowest point. With a small learning rate the trail settles into the bottom. Above 2 divided by the steepness, the ball jumps across the steep direction, lands higher each time, and leaves the surface. A dark blue ghost trail keeps the previous run for comparison.
assumptions: Illustration: an idealised bowl-shaped loss, not a real trained model.

Loss = (steepness·x² + z²)/2, with x the steep direction and z the gentle one (steepness 1). The surface is drawn at 0.25 × loss, and it narrows along x as steepness rises so its rim stays at the same height. The readouts show the true loss.
Each step moves the ball by −learning rate × slope. There is no momentum and no noise. The arrow shows the next step at its true length, in the same units as the surface.

Along x, each step multiplies the distance from the bottom by (1 − rate × steepness). If that factor's size is above 1 (rate above 2/steepness), the distance grows every step. This is exact for this bowl.

Every run starts at x = 0.6, z = 2.2. A run stops when the ball leaves the drawn surface (diverged), when the loss falls below 0.001 (converged), or after 60 steps (step limit). After it diverges, the ball and trail are drawn at the rim.
Changing the learning rate starts a new run and keeps the old path as the ghost. Changing the steepness starts a new run and clears the ghost, because the bowl's shape changes.

blocks.text:
I'm not passing this scene. The maths is right, but one claim in the description is false and one label names an arrow too small to see.

**What checks out.** I recomputed the numbers in the traces and they all match.
- **Start:** loss is 3.14 at x = 0.6, z = 2.2, steepness 4.
- **Learning rate 0.7:** x goes 0.6 → −1.08 → 1.944. The ball leaves the surface after 2 steps with loss 7.578, and the stretch factor is −1.80.
- **Learning rate 0.19:** after 14 steps the loss is 0.0066, and the stretch factor is 0.24.
- **Arrow:** it points the right way and is drawn at its true length.
- **Request values:** every range, step and default matches the plan.

**Problems that need fixing:**
1. **False claim (major, all captures).** The description says the ball "lands higher each time" when it diverges. The program doesn't do that. The first step always lowers the loss, because the gentle direction is still shrinking:
   - default rate 0.55: loss goes from 3.14 to 1.53, and only then grows (1.64, …);
   - rate 0.7: loss goes from 3.14 to 2.55, then 7.58.

   Only the distance along the steep direction grows every step. The fix is to reword the description, or add a readout for the steep-direction distance or its share of the loss.
2. **"Next step" label on an invisible arrow (major, both 0.19 captures).** Near convergence the step is about 0.02 long, so the arrow can't be seen but the label stays the same size. It reads as a label for nothing. It also crowds the "Lowest point" label. The label should hide, or shrink with the arrow, when the step is tiny.

**Minor points:**
- **Diverged ball off the surface:** after diverging, the ball is drawn at x = 1.575, past the surface edge at 1.5, and above the rim. It floats there touching the "Steep direction" label, which is placed in the same spot.
- **Direction labels:** "Steep direction" and "Gentle direction" are floating text with no axis line or arrow, so it isn't clear which way they mean.
